references.text: The same pattern is repeated in the parable of the lost coin: The woman calls together her friends and neighbors and asks them to rejoice with her because she has found what was lost ([ref:Luk 15:9|Luke 15:9]).
In the parable of the prodigal son, there is likewise great celebration when the son returns home, parallel to the joy over the recovered sheep ([ref:Luk 15:23-24|Luke 15:23-24]).
Jesus applies the parable directly: There is greater joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who do not need repentance ([ref:Luk 15:7|Luke 15:7]).

The context for the celebration: The shepherd leaves the ninety-nine and searches until he finds the lost sheep, places it on his shoulders, and carries it home with joy ([ref:Luk 15:4-5|Luke 15:4-5]).

God himself promises through Ezekiel to search for his lost sheep, rescue them, and bring them back – the background for Jesus' parable of the good shepherd who seeks what is lost ([ref:Esek 34:11-16|Ezekiel 34:11-16]).

The prophet Isaiah describes the Lord as a shepherd who tends his flock, gathers the lambs in his arms, and carries them close to his heart – an image of God's care for the lost ([ref:Jes 40:11|Isaiah 40:11]).
Matthew's parallel to the parable of the lost sheep: Jesus emphasizes that it is not the Father's will that even one of these little ones should be lost ([ref:Matt 18:12-14|Matthew 18:12-14]).

The Lord your God is in your midst, a mighty savior. He rejoices over you with gladness; he is quiet in his love; he exults over you with singing – God's own joy in saving the lost ([ref:Sef 3:17|Zephaniah 3:17]).
Peter uses the image of stray sheep who have returned to their shepherd and overseer, echoing the joy over the recovered sheep ([ref:1 Pet 2:25|1 Peter 2:25]).

Jesus summarizes the parable of the lost coin by saying there is joy among God's angels over one sinner who repents – the same principle as in verse 6 regarding the joy over the recovered sheep ([ref:Luk 15:10|Luke 15:10]).
